nameStory: This jumping spider carries the name 'Hakka' from its scientific classification, which references the Hakka people of East Asia where this species originates. The species name 'himeshimensis' comes from the Himeshima region of Japan, highlighting its far-from-home journey to New England's rocky shores.
description: The Hakka jumping spider is a small, compact arachnid that made an impressive leap across the Pacific to establish itself along New England's coastline. Like all jumping spiders, it has a sturdy, almost box-like body shape and remarkably large forward-facing eyes that give it an almost curious expression. These spiders are relatively small, typically measuring less than half an inch in body length, but what they lack in size they make up for in agility and hunting prowess.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front eyes arranged in a row across the face, with the middle pair notably larger and giving an almost telescope-like appearance - you can often see light reflecting off them like tiny mirrors

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rectangular body that feels firm and slightly fuzzy to the touch, like a tiny velvet-covered box with sturdy legs

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in characteristic quick, jerky hops and will often turn to face you directly when approached, seeming to study you with those prominent eyes

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates small, silken retreat sacs tucked into rock crevices rather than hunting webs - these feel like tiny silk sleeping bags when gently touched

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to easily sit on a dime with room to spare, but stockier and more robust-looking than many other tiny spiders

habitat: Look for these spiders in rocky coastal areas throughout New England, particularly where granite ledges and stone outcroppings meet the influence of salt air. They favor the nooks and crannies of sea cliffs, rocky shorelines, and even coastal stone walls where they can tuck their silk retreats into protected crevices. The combination of sun-warmed rocks and the moderating influence of ocean breezes creates ideal conditions for these heat-loving immigrants.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots in rock crevices and become active on warm, sunny days when the rocks heat up.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you're most likely to spot them hunting on sun-warmed stone surfaces, with mating displays and egg-laying occurring.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, preparing winter retreats and laying final egg sacs before cold weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in rock crevices in silk-lined chambers, completely inactive until spring warmth returns to the coastal stones.

funFact: These tiny spiders are accomplished intercontinental travelers that likely arrived in New England as stowaways on cargo ships, then successfully colonized our rocky coastlines despite being thousands of miles from their ancestral Asian homes - making them some of our newest naturalized New Englanders!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small jumping spiders, but the coastal rocky habitat is a dead giveaway - few other jumping spiders specifically seek out seaside stone environments. Remember: 'Hakka on the rocks' - if you find a jumping spider on coastal stones, it's likely this species.
contextualKnowledge: As a relatively recent introduction to North America, this species represents an ongoing example of how global trade continues to reshape local ecosystems, though these spiders appear to fill a niche without displacing native species.
compareHints: Since this is the only Hakka species in our region, compare it to other small jumping spiders in the Salticidae family. Hakka jumping spiders are distinguished by their specific preference for rocky coastal habitats, whereas most other New England jumping spiders prefer gardens, forests, or grasslands. The habitat preference combined with their compact build and prominent eyes makes identification fairly straightforward once you know where to look.
